passage:
Hemant: Omkar, I am at the hardware shop and the owner only speaks Bengali. I need a hinge for the cupboard
Omkar: Show him the broken one
Hemant: I did. Then I drew a little door with my finger, opening and closing 😅
Omkar: And?
Hemant: He gave me a lock. Wrong thing
Omkar: Take a photo of the hinge and show it, then say "this one" and point
Hemant: Good idea. Also he nodded in a way I could not read. Yes or no?
Omkar: Ask again with the photo
Hemant: Done. He is smiling and opening a drawer. Fingers crossed 🤞

qa.a: He needed a hinge for the cupboard.

qa.q: Why was Hemant unsure about the owner's nod, and what did he feel?
qa.a: He could not read whether the nod meant yes or no, and he was uneasy after being handed the wrong item. The nod might have been polite or confirming, so he wanted to check.

qa.q: What did Omkar suggest to avoid another mistake?
qa.a: He suggested showing a photo of the hinge and saying "this one" while pointing, so the request is confirmed with an image.

qa.q: How might the shop owner have felt when Hemant mimed a door?
qa.a: He may have felt willing to help but uncertain what Hemant wanted, which is why he offered a lock instead.

grounding: Chat about a worker in a new city using shapes, mime and pointing to make a request and checking with a photo to avoid mix-ups.

subtype: Describing with hands to bridge language gaps [Regulating]
passage: Kamal had just started at the brick kiln outside Ranchi, and his Hindi was thin. On his second morning he needed a wheelbarrow with a flat tyre swapped. He pointed at the wheel, made a hissing sound and spread his hands to show air going out. The foreman, Rukmini's uncle, understood and waved him toward the shed. But when Kamal drew a circle in the air to mean "wheel", the man beside him thought he meant the whole team should circle up. They laughed together. Kamal took out his phone, showed a picture of the tyre and said, "Yeh?" The uncle nodded. "Haan, yeh." The tyre was changed within minutes.

qa.q: Where did Kamal start work?
qa.a: He started at a brick kiln outside Ranchi.

qa.q: What did Kamal's picture and "Yeh?" show about his thinking?
qa.a: It showed he wanted to be sure the request was understood, since his air circle had been misread. The laughing suggests the mix-up was harmless.

qa.q: What worked to make his request clear?
qa.a: A phone picture of the tyre and the confirming word "Yeh?" made the request clear after the gestures caused confusion.

qa.q: How might the man beside Kamal have understood the circle in the air?
qa.a: He thought Kamal meant the team should circle up, so he took the gesture as a call to gather.

grounding: Third-person rural narrative of a worker in a new place using mime and pointing that can mislead, confirmed with an image.

subtype: Describing with hands to bridge language gaps [Regulating]
passage: Felix had been in Valencia for nine days, and his Spanish stopped at "hola" and "gracias". At the hardware shop near his flat he needed wall plugs for the shelves he was fitting. He held up one finger, twisted the other hand around it, then mimed pushing something into the wall. Diego, behind the counter, nodded eagerly and came back with a box of hinges. Felix laughed and shook his head. Diego tried again: a screwdriver. Now they were both grinning, a little helpless. Felix stopped miming. He pulled out his notebook, sketched a small ribbed plug with a screw going into it and a wall behind, then held up four fingers and pointed at the sketch. "Four?" Diego asked, writing a 4 beside the drawing. "These?" He reached under the counter. Exactly right. Felix wrote "gracias" under the drawing and underlined it twice.

qa.q: What did Felix need at the hardware shop?
qa.a: Wall plugs for the shelves he was fitting.

qa.q: What was Felix feeling when Diego brought the screwdriver?
qa.a: Felix felt amused but a little helpless and frustrated, since the mime kept being read as something else.

qa.q: What fixed the misunderstanding?
qa.a: A quick sketch of the plug and screw plus a number, which Diego confirmed by writing 4 and asking 'These?' before handing it over.

qa.q: How might Diego have experienced the miming?
qa.a: Diego wanted to help and kept guessing, probably feeling a bit embarrassed at getting it wrong twice, then relieved when the sketch made it clear.

grounding: Shows a worker in a new city using mime to ask for an item, the gesture misleading, and a sketch and confirming check fixing it.

subtype: Describing with hands to bridge language gaps [Regulating]
passage: On her third night at the working women's hostel in Kolkata, Sudha needed to press her shirt for her first day at the lab. The warden, Gargi-di, spoke Bangla and some Hindi; Sudha's Hindi was shaky and her Bangla non-existent. At the office window, Sudha pinched her collar, then slid her flat palm back and forth over an invisible surface. Gargi-di's face lit up. She reached behind her and handed over a mop and bucket. Sudha burst out laughing, and so did Gargi-di, though neither knew exactly why yet. Sudha set the mop down, found a picture of an iron on her phone and held it up next to her creased sleeve. "Istri!" Gargi-di said. "Istri?" Sudha repeated carefully, pointing at the photo. Gargi-di nodded, unlocked a cupboard and brought out an iron. "Ten o'clock, back," she said, tapping her watch.

qa.q: What did Gargi-di hand over first?
qa.a: A mop and bucket.

qa.q: What was Sudha feeling when she was handed the mop?
qa.a: Sudha felt amused and a bit sheepish 😅, realising the pressing mime looked like floor cleaning, with some worry underneath about the creased shirt for her first day.

qa.q: What helped Sudha get the right thing?
qa.a: Showing a picture of an iron next to her creased sleeve and repeating the word 'Istri' back to confirm it.

qa.q: How might Gargi-di have understood the palm sliding back and forth?
qa.a: Gargi-di read it as wiping or mopping, a sensible guess from the gesture alone, which is why a picture helped.

grounding: Shows a worker new to a city miming a request across a language gap, the mime misleading, and a picture plus a repeated word confirming it.

subtype: Describing with hands to bridge language gaps [Regulating]
passage:
Hi Darshan,
You asked how I'm managing in Busan with about twelve words of Korean. Mostly with my hands, which went badly on Sunday.
I needed a big cooking pot, the kind for rice for eight people when my team comes over. At the market I made a huge circle with both arms and then stirred the air. The shop owner nodded and pulled out a plastic washing tub. I shook my head, pointed at my mouth and mimed eating. He brought out a steamer basket.
So I stopped, typed "large cooking pot" into my translation app, and showed him a photo of Ammi's big pot from my gallery. He laughed, said a word I didn't catch, and brought the right one. Before paying, I pointed at it and said, "This one, yes?" He nodded.
Lesson: hands start the conversation, pictures finish it.
Afreen

qa.q: What did the shop owner bring out first?
qa.a: A plastic washing tub.

qa.q: How was Afreen feeling as the gestures kept going wrong?
qa.a: Afreen was probably frustrated but amused, laughing about it in the email; being misread twice may also have felt a little embarrassing.

qa.q: Which steps finally worked, and why?
qa.a: Typing the words into a translation app, showing a photo of Ammi's pot, and checking 'This one, yes?' before paying, because a picture and a confirming phrase remove the guesswork.

qa.q: How might the shop owner have understood the big circle and stirring?
qa.a: He likely read something large and round for washing, a fair guess, then a steamer when eating was mimed, since the same gestures fit several objects.

grounding: Shows a worker in a new country using shapes and mime to ask for an item, being misread, and a photo and confirming phrase preventing a mistake.

subtype: Describing with hands to bridge language gaps [Regulating]
passage:
Rafiq, you'll laugh. My second week in Chennai, my Tamil was about six words, and I needed a mop. At the hardware shop I told the owner, "Hello, I'm Payal, new in the building upstairs," and then I started acting. Hands gripping a stick, pushing it back and forth across the floor. He nodded, very confident, and brought me... a broom. I did it again, bigger, even made a squeezing motion for the bucket. He brought a bucket. Just a bucket.
Then I remembered my phone. I found a photo of a mop, held it up and said, "This one?" He laughed so hard, slapped his forehead, and said the Tamil word slowly for me, twice. Now I point, show a picture, and then check: "This? Yes?" It saves a lot of brooms.

qa.q: What did the shop owner bring the first time Payal mimed?
qa.a: He brought a broom.

qa.q: How do you think Payal felt when the owner brought just a bucket?
qa.a: Payal probably felt frustrated and a bit embarrassed, though the way the story is told suggests it also felt funny looking back. 😅

qa.q: What does Payal do now to avoid mix-ups?
qa.a: Point, show a picture on the phone, and then check with "This? Yes?" before buying.

qa.q: How might the shop owner have seen the miming?
qa.a: He seemed confident he understood each time, so the mime misled him until the photo made it clear, which is why he laughed and taught the word.

grounding: A worker new to a city uses mime and pointing to ask for something, finds gestures can mislead, and checks with a picture and a confirming phrase.
